What the spec step said it changed, its final output:

You're right, and the earlier rule was mine. I wrote that a chain stays "Running" until every step it might send is done. So any chain whose code step was never sent, like old ones or ones interrupted by closing the app, was stuck Running for good. I replaced that rule. `piton check` and `piton build` ran clean.

- **Running only when a step is running now:** a chain reads Running exactly while one of its steps is building, compiling or running in the app at that moment, never otherwise.
- **Queued:** if no step is running but one is waiting in the queue, the chain reads Queued and sits in the Queued group.
- **Otherwise it's over:**
  - It reads Failed or Cancelled if a step was. Otherwise it takes its last step's own status: Done, or Not recorded if that step has no record of its run.
  - A chain whose code step was never sent shows that as a muted note on its parent row, never as Running.
- **Reading state correctly:**
  - Each step's state comes from where it actually is. It's running only while the app has its run going, which no step from the history can be after a restart. It's queued only while its prompt is in the queue. Otherwise it comes from its own history record.
  - Steps are joined to a chain only by which step each was sent from, so a task never picks up another chain's state.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `PromptEditor` `#chained-tasks`, `TasksTabScope` `#description` and `#rows` for which group a chain sits in, and `MessageList` `#status`.

49:Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was: behind every prompt waiting there that was sent before its chain, earlier chains' steps included, and ahead of every prompt sent after it. So a chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt, or another chain's code step, sent before the chain was, and a Code prompt sent while the chain's spec step ran waits for the chain's code step rather than coming between the chain's steps. Two steps whose chains were sent in the same order run in that order, whichever spec step finished first. Where nothing sent before its chain is waiting, it runs as soon as its lane is free, and straight away if it already is. Its place holds however it came to be queued, so a restart, with the queue read back from the project, keeps it there. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
51:In the previous tasks list, a chain's steps are grouped under one parent item, so they read as parts of a single chain. The parent is a heading row in the list, tinted the Chain colour, as the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, a little more strongly than a single task's tint: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is the chain's as a whole, worked out only from its steps as they actually are, never from what the chain might still do: Running, with its spinner and its time counting, exactly while one of its steps is building, compiling, or running now, in this project's runs, and at no other time. Otherwise, while one of its steps waits in a lane's queue, it reads Queued, in the theme's muted colour, and is listed with the queued prompts. Otherwise it is over, whether or not it ever sent every step it might have: Failed or Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise its last step's own status, Done, or Not recorded for one with no record of its run. A chain whose later step was never sent, as one from before chains sent them or one whose application closed between its steps, is over, its parent saying muted after its step count that its code step was never sent, and never reads Running for it.
52:Each step's state is read from where it truly is: a step is running only while the application has its run under way, which no step from the history ever does after a restart, since every run ends when the application quits; queued only while its prompt is in the queue; and otherwise from its own history record, a step with no record of its run reading Not recorded, never Running. Steps are joined to their chain only by which step each was sent from, as below, so a task never takes the state of a chain it doesn't belong to, and a chain never counts a task that isn't one of its steps.
53:While a chain is Running, it is listed in the Running group of the right sidebar's Tasks tab, with all its steps beneath it; while Queued, in the Queued group; and once over, among the previous tasks. It has no checkbox, Resend, or Send to the other mode of its own, and clicking it doesn't open anything.
54:Beneath it, each step stays an item of its own, exactly as any previous task is, with its checkbox, status, Resend, and whatever else a task offers, opening onto its own prompt, table, and changed files. The steps are indented from the parent, joined to it by a thin line in the Chain colour down their left, from the parent's heading to the last step, and each is labelled by what it did, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour, before its prompt, which leaves out the prompt's first line when it is the parent's. They are listed in the order they ran.
55:A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it, and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent saying the rest is the latest task. A session divider never falls between a chain's steps: it goes above the chain's parent. A step from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.
59:The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent, and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping follow it. The header shows its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.
15:The right sidebar's Tasks tab: every task of the project at a glance, what has run, what is running, and what is queued, where any of them can be looked into, edited, and adjusted, and a chain given more steps.
26:Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in its mode's colour, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, then its status, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued, its place in the queue, then the first line of its prompt, cut off with an ellipsis, then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has been running, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes it. A chain is one row, its steps as rows indented beneath it, collapsed to start with, as the previous tasks group a chain. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.
30:The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, group headings and a chain's expanded steps included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
31:A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its chain expanded or not, its selection and highlight kept.
43:#### Chain Steps
38:Among the previous tasks, every task's heading shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.
44:The header heads the view with every task under way, not only the latest, that is the latest task, and every other task building, compiling, or running, as when a Spec task and a Code task run in their two lanes at once, or a chain's step runs beside a task of the other lane. Only one of them is selected at a time, and only it is shown in full, with its header as a task's header always is, its compiled prompt, hidden anchor's name, status label and elapsed time, and buttons, and beneath it its output table and the files it changed. The others are compact rows, one each, stacked above the selected task's header, in the order they were sent, oldest at the top. With only one task to show, there are no compact rows, and the header is just as it was.
63:A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.
76:Each task in the previous tasks list hints at the mode it was sent in: its heading's background is a faint tint of that mode's colour, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), red for Code, purple for Chain, blue for Spec, green for Ask, and grey for Freeform, far fainter than the latest task's header, so the list reads as a column of the list's own background with each task only touched by its colour. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the history that doesn't say, keeps the list's background untinted. Its status label, prompt, checkbox, and buttons stay readable over the tint, in light and dark mode, and its hover and open states still show over it. An open task's prompt and output beneath its heading are not tinted.

#### Status

##### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

##### Elapsed

Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the second its history file is named by to when its record was written, with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.
Among the previous tasks, every task's heading shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.

content.text:
You're right, and the stuck chains were caused by my earlier rule, not your data. I had made a chain count as running until every step it might send was done, so any chain whose code step was never sent stayed "Running" forever. Now a chain reads Running only while one of its steps is actually running. All tests pass, including a new test for this rule; I haven't checked it against your project in the app.

- **Running:** only while a step is building, compiling or running right now. A task loaded from history can never count, because after a restart its run is marked as ended.
- **Queued:** if nothing is running but one of the chain's steps is waiting in the queue, the chain reads "Queued" in muted text and is listed in the Queued group.
- **Otherwise it's over:** it reads Failed or Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise takes its last step's own status (Done, or Not recorded if that step has no record).
- **Chains with only a spec step:** they now sit in Previous with the spec step's status. The parent row adds a muted "code step never sent" (or "spec follow-up never sent") after its step count.

On reading the data: steps are still joined to a chain only by which step each was sent from, so a task can't pick up another chain's state. A step's own status comes from its history record, so nothing from the history can show as running.

The changes are in `src/prompt_mode/tasks_tab.rs`, plus the chain status and time functions in `src/prompt_mode.rs`. This follows the updated spec, which matches what you asked.
